question: How does Mengelberg shape a phrase within one disc side?
intro: This is the first historical side of Mengelberg’s Concertgebouw recording, not the complete first movement. Commons dates the session to 1939–40 and the first release to 1941. The source is left intact; its ending is a disc-side boundary, not Beethoven’s final cadence.

cues.title: One historical side
cues.text: Only the first of the movement’s two files is used here. The player streams that original file; no joined reconstruction has been made.

cues.title: The recorded texture turns
cues.text: A prominent measured boundary falls here. Compare the spacing and weight of the phrase with the same passage in the other performances, rather than comparing the files’ total lengths.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/beethoven-5-first-mengelberg-side1.txt: novelty48 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: The largest change
cues.text: This is the side’s strongest measured change in pitch content and texture. It provides a useful listening landmark, but does not establish a precise bar number.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/beethoven-5-first-mengelberg-side1.txt: maximum novelty188 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: A crest before the break
cues.text: The side’s loudest average five seconds lie close to its ending. Do not hear the approaching cutoff as a composed ending: Beethoven’s movement continues on another side.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
